description: We’re a team of  Data Professionals from Myanmar, with a shared interest in geospatial data, data science, and astrophysics. We’re passionate about exploring the intersection of data, science, and technology, especially in the field of space exploration. We enjoy learning, experimenting with new ideas, and using data to uncover insights and solve interesting challenges. We’re excited to be part of this journey and see what we can discover together!
summary:
TerraTwin is a three-phase planetary analog discovery project that helps users find Earth landscapes resembling locations on Mars or the Moon.

In Phase 1, we compared Mars imagery from NASA Mars Trek with cloud-filtered Earth imagery from Asia, Africa, and Australia. We removed water and built-up areas using ESA WorldCover, converted the images into DINOv2 embeddings, and ranked the most visually similar Mars-Earth image pairs.

In Phase 2, we developed the Jezero Analog Finder. Using Jezero Crater as a reference, we compared elevation, relief, slope, roughness, vegetation, land cover, and thermal behavior with dry Earth regions. Large areas were screened in Google Earth Engine, unsuitable locations were removed, and the strongest candidates were validated using more detailed elevation data.

In Phase 3, we created a general Moon-and-Mars terrain search system. Planetary locations are compared with an Earth catalog containing imagery, elevation, slope, land cover, soil, and material information. The system can return ranked Earth candidates using visual, geometric, and physical similarities.

TerraTwin addresses the challenge by turning large, complex planetary datasets into understandable and explainable Earth comparisons. This is important because Earth analogs can support planetary research, mission planning, field testing, education, and public exploration.
details:
Project Details

TerraTwin is a three-phase planetary analog discovery platform that helps people find Earth landscapes resembling locations on Mars or the Moon. The project combines visual image matching, scientific terrain analysis, and explainable similarity search. TerraTwin began as an experiment for comparing Mars and Earth imagery, then developed into a detailed search for Earth landscapes similar to Jezero Crater, and finally expanded into a reusable planetary exploration system for both Mars and the Moon.

How It Works

The first phase explored visual similarity between Mars and Earth. Mars images came from the NASA Mars Trek Viking global color mosaic, while Earth images came from Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 data. We collected Earth imagery from Asia, Africa, and Australia, reduced cloud contamination, and used ESA WorldCover data to remove areas dominated by water or built-up land. We then used the DINOv2 Base model to convert the Mars and Earth images into numerical representations called embeddings. These embeddings allowed the system to measure visual similarity and rank the Earth images that looked most similar to selected Mars regions. The phase produced the top three Earth matches for each search region, together with coordinates and side-by-side image comparisons.

The second phase developed the Jezero Analog Finder, which introduced a more scientific and explainable comparison centered on Jezero Crater. We described Jezero using elevation variation, relative relief, slope, flat-ground coverage, surface roughness, and thermal behavior. We then used Google Earth Engine to screen dry regions across Africa, the Middle East, and Australia. Areas containing too much vegetation, water, ice, cropland, or built-up land were removed. The strongest candidates were studied again in smaller areas and at a finer terrain resolution. We visually reviewed the top candidates to remove false positives such as farms, mines, reservoirs, settlements, or cells containing several unrelated landscape types. The accepted finalists were then validated again using more detailed Earth elevation data. The final ranking combined detailed terrain similarity, the candidate’s weakest terrain feature, and a relative thermal-response comparison. This phase produced three validated Earth candidates, including a leading location with a final score of 83.5% and terrain similarity of 90.8%.

The third phase expands TerraTwin into a general Moon-and-Mars terrain analog explorer. A user can select an indexed location on the Moon or Mars and choose either geometry-based or functional similarity. The geometry model focuses on terrain shape, while the functional model also considers physical and material context. A vector-search system compares the planetary location with 4,096 indexed Earth candidates and returns the top five or top ten matches. Each result can include coordinates, surface imagery, elevation, slope, terrain information, and supporting comparison details. This makes the final results more understandable than a system that returns only a similarity score.

Data and Development Tools

TerraTwin combines several planetary and Earth-observation datasets. Mars data include NASA Mars Trek imagery, MOLA elevation data, TES thermal-inertia data, and CTX orbital imagery. Moon data include lunar surface imagery, elevation, terrain shape, slope, available spectral or material information, and physical context. Earth data include Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 imagery, ASTER GDEM and SRTM elevation, NASA GIBS imagery, ESA WorldCover land-cover information, SoilGrids 2.0 soil and material properties, and MODIS vegetation and temperature measurements.

The project was developed using Python and JavaScript. JavaScript was used in Google Earth Engine to process large satellite datasets, divide search regions into geographic cells, apply cloud and land-cover filters, calculate terrain and temperature summaries, and export candidate information. Python was used to prepare the datasets, create DINOv2 embeddings, calculate visual and terrain similarity, validate terrain statistics, perform FAISS vector searches, rank the candidates, and create maps and comparison visualizations. Jupyter notebooks were used to organize the analysis into clear and reproducible stages. The project did not require specialized hardware because large satellite-processing tasks were completed in Google Earth Engine, while model inference and analysis could run on standard development computers or cloud computing resources.

Benefits and Intended Impact

TerraTwin makes complex planetary and Earth-observation data easier to explore. Without a system like TerraTwin, researchers or students may need to examine thousands of images, terrain maps, and scientific measurements manually. TerraTwin reduces this work by returning a short, ranked list of Earth locations with comparable visual, terrain, or physical characteristics.

The project could support planetary research, analog field-site selection, geological and astrobiological comparisons, and the planning of rover, sensor, and operational tests. It could also help mission teams identify Earth environments suitable for testing equipment under terrain conditions that resemble selected areas of Mars or the Moon. For students, educators, and the public, TerraTwin offers a more accessible way to explore planetary landscapes and understand how Earth can be used to study other worlds. Because the platform can support several planetary bodies and additional datasets, the same approach could be extended to future missions and new planetary targets.

Creativity and Team Considerations

TerraTwin is creative because it combines three complementary approaches within one project: computer-vision similarity, science-based terrain validation, and fast vector retrieval. The system does not rely only on whether two images look alike. A location may appear visually similar to Mars but still be rejected if it is dominated by farms, cities, water, ice, mining, or an unsuitable terrain structure. This combination makes the results more reliable and explainable than a purely visual matching system.

During development, the team considered differences in image resolution between Earth, Mars, and the Moon, as well as clouds, missing observations, and differences in image quality. We also considered contamination from agriculture, water, ice, buildings, and other human-modified surfaces. Terrain measurements were compared at more consistent scales, and geographic-separation rules were applied so that the final recommendations did not all come from neighboring locations.

The team also considered explainability and responsible interpretation. Each result includes supporting information such as coordinates, imagery, elevation, slope, terrain features, and comparison scores. The platform includes safeguards for coordinates outside the indexed catalog and distinguishes terrain resemblance from exact geological equivalence. A strong TerraTwin result should therefore be described as a candidate planetary analog, not as proof that the Earth location has the same geology, materials, or history as the selected location on Mars or the Moon.

Overall, TerraTwin addresses the challenge by transforming large and complex planetary datasets into an understandable discovery experience. The intended impact is a flexible platform that allows researchers, mission planners, educators, students, and curious users to move from a location on the Moon or Mars to meaningful, ranked, and evidence-supported Earth comparisons.
